title: Python
text: Python is a readable general-purpose language widely used for data science, machine learning, automation, scripting and web back ends (Flask, Django). It is a common first language because the syntax is close to plain English. Good starting points are the official tutorial and a project-based course. Practise by automating small tasks, then move to Pandas or Flask depending on your target career.

title: Java
text: Java is a statically typed, object-oriented language used in enterprise back ends and Android development (alongside Kotlin). Learning Java strengthens object-oriented programming, data structures and typing concepts that transfer to other languages.

title: JavaScript and TypeScript
text: JavaScript runs in every browser and, with Node.js, on servers. Learn HTML and CSS first, then core JavaScript (variables, functions, the DOM, asynchronous code), then a framework such as React. TypeScript adds static types on top of JavaScript and is common in larger codebases.

title: C and C++
text: C and C++ give close control over memory and performance. They are used in systems programming, game engines, embedded software and competitive programming. They are harder for beginners; learn the concepts of pointers, memory and object-oriented design step by step.

title: SQL and databases
text: SQL is the standard language for relational databases such as MySQL. Core topics are SELECT queries, joins, aggregation, subqueries, indexes, constraints and normalisation. SQL appears in almost every data and back-end role, so it is one of the highest-value skills to learn early.

title: Git and GitHub
text: Git is the version-control tool used by almost all software teams. Learn commit, branch, merge, pull request and resolving conflicts. A GitHub profile with well-documented projects works as a portfolio for fresher job applications.

title: Data structures and algorithms
text: Data structures (arrays, lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, hash tables) and algorithms (searching, sorting, recursion, dynamic programming) are tested in many technical interviews. Practise regularly with a few problems per week, and explain your reasoning aloud.

title: Web development roadmap
text: A common path is HTML and CSS, then JavaScript, then a frontend framework (React), then a back-end language and framework (Node.js or Python with Flask), then databases and deployment. Build small projects at every stage and publish them on GitHub.

title: Software development practices
text: Professional software development involves version control, code review, automated testing, documentation and agile ways of working. Students can practise by contributing to open-source projects, writing tests for their own projects and using issue trackers.

title: Data science learning path
text: Data science combines programming (Python), statistics, data handling (NumPy, Pandas, SQL), visualisation and machine learning. A practical order is Python, then Pandas and SQL, then statistics, then supervised machine learning with scikit-learn, then a portfolio of end-to-end projects with clear written conclusions.

title: Data analyst vs data scientist
text: Data analysts focus on SQL, spreadsheets, dashboards and communicating business insights. Data scientists add more statistics and machine learning. Many people start as analysts and move toward data science. Both roles value clear communication.

title: Machine learning basics
text: Machine learning builds models that learn patterns from data. Supervised learning predicts labels (classification, regression); unsupervised learning finds structure (clustering). Key habits are splitting data into train and test sets, validating with cross-validation, and avoiding data leakage.

title: Deep learning and generative AI
text: Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks for images, text and speech. Frameworks include PyTorch and TensorFlow. Large language models are built on the transformer architecture. Prerequisites are Python, linear algebra, probability and classical machine learning.

title: Cloud computing and DevOps
text: Cloud computing provides on-demand servers, storage and services over the internet. DevOps combines development and operations using automation: containers (Docker), orchestration (Kubernetes), CI/CD pipelines and monitoring. Start with Linux, networking and Git, then containers, then a cloud provider's fundamentals.

title: Cybersecurity
text: Cybersecurity covers protecting systems, networks and data. Build a base in networking, Linux and operating systems, then learn security fundamentals, common web vulnerabilities (OWASP Top 10) and cryptography basics. Only practise offensive techniques on systems you own or in legal practice labs.

title: Mobile app development
text: Android apps are mainly written in Kotlin (Java is also supported). Cross-platform frameworks such as Flutter let one codebase target several platforms. Learn the app lifecycle, UI layouts, local storage and calling REST APIs.

title: UI/UX design
text: UI/UX designers research users, create wireframes and prototypes, and test usability. Build a portfolio of two to three case studies showing your process, not just final screens. Figma is a widely used design tool.

title: Software testing and QA
text: QA engineers verify software quality through manual testing and automation. Learn test design, bug reporting, SQL, and an automation tool such as Selenium with a language like Python. Good bug reports are clear, reproducible and prioritised.

title: Higher education options after a computer science degree
text: Common options after a bachelor's degree are working first, a master's programme (for example M.Sc, MCA or M.Tech depending on your background), or research degrees. Entry requirements, entrance exams, fees and deadlines differ by university and country and change every year, so always confirm them on the institution's official admissions page before deciding. A master's degree is most useful for research-oriented roles such as data science and AI; many software roles value projects and skills as much as degrees.

title: Entry-level certifications
text: Certifications can validate skills but do not replace projects. Popular entry-level options include cloud fundamentals (AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner, Microsoft Azure Fundamentals), CompTIA Security+ for security, Google certificates for data analytics and UX design, and ISTQB for testing. Exam content and fees change, so check the issuing organisation's page.

title: Technical interview preparation
text: Prepare in four parts: (1) fundamentals of your main language, (2) data structures and algorithms practice, (3) your own projects - be ready to explain design decisions and trade-offs, and (4) behavioural answers using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Do mock interviews with friends and think aloud while solving problems.

title: Resume tips for freshers
text: Keep a fresher resume to one page. Include a short summary, skills grouped by category, two to four projects with the technologies used and measurable outcomes where honest, education, internships and certifications, and links to GitHub or LinkedIn. Tailor the skills section to each job description and avoid listing tools you cannot discuss.

title: Building a portfolio and getting experience
text: Employers look for evidence of skill. Build three to five projects with README files, publish them on GitHub, contribute to open-source where possible, and apply for internships. Hackathons and student projects also count. Quality and clear explanation matter more than quantity.

title: Communication and soft skills
text: Clear written and spoken communication, teamwork and the ability to learn quickly are valued in every technical role. Practise by writing project documentation, explaining concepts to peers and presenting your projects.

title: Salary and job-market information
text: Salaries and hiring demand vary widely by country, city, company, experience and skills, and they change over time. This assistant does not quote salary figures because they cannot be verified here. For reliable numbers, consult official labour-statistics sources, recent job postings in your target location and company-reported ranges.

title: How to choose a career path
text: Start from your interests and strengths, test them with small projects, and compare the skills each career requires with what you already have. Skill-gap analysis helps you decide what to learn first. Recommendations from any tool are guidance, not guarantees; talk to mentors and professionals before deciding.
